opus-5.5.text:
I think open-sourcing has become quite important for us at this stage, for a few reasons.

The first is technical. When you release a model openly, you get feedback from a much larger and more diverse group of people than you could ever reach internally. Developers and researchers push the model in directions you didn't anticipate. They find failure modes, they build tools on top of it, and they tell you very directly what works and what doesn't. That feedback loop makes the model better faster.

The second is about trust and recognition. For a company like ours, it's not enough to say we have a strong model. People need to be able to verify it themselves. Open-sourcing lets the global community evaluate the model on its own merits. If it's genuinely good, that speaks louder than any benchmark we publish. It also helps a lot with attracting talent, because strong researchers want to work on things that the world can see and use.

The third is the ecosystem. I believe the long-term value of foundation models will come from the applications and agents built on top of them. Open-sourcing lowers the barrier for many people to build those things, and that expands the pie for everyone, including us. A model that many people build on becomes a kind of standard, and that position is very valuable.

Of course, there are trade-offs. You give away some things that could have been a short-term advantage. But I don't think the moat in this field comes from hiding the weights. It comes from continuously improving the model, the capability to train the next generation, and how well you understand what users really need. If you're confident in your ability to keep moving forward, open-sourcing isn't really a loss. It's more like putting your best work out there and then running ahead of it.

So for us, open source isn't just a marketing choice. It's part of how we want to push the frontier, together with the community rather than in isolation.

r001.rationale: The response says community feedback can help improve the model, but does not state that improving the base model itself appears limited to its original developer.

r002.rationale: It discusses community-built applications and agents, but does not identify agentic post-training on open-source models as a way the community could contribute to model improvement.

fable-5.1.text:
Open-sourcing, for us, is less an ideological choice than a practical one about where we are in the race. If you are not the absolute frontier, the most valuable thing you can do is make sure your technology gets used and improved by as many people as possible. A closed model that is second-best gets no attention. An open model that is second-best becomes the thing everyone builds on, and that network effect compounds.

There are a few concrete layers to it. The first is tech and talent. When you open the weights and, more importantly, the technical report, you get feedback from thousands of researchers who find things you missed. People fine-tune it, break it, benchmark it against everything. That is free evaluation at a scale no internal team can match. It also makes recruiting easier, because strong researchers want to work on things the community actually sees.

The second is distribution. For a company like ours, consumer product and open model reinforce each other. The model sets the reputation, the product converts it. Developers who pick up the open weights become the people who later recommend the API or build on top of our stack.

The third is honesty about moats. I don't think the moat in this industry is the weights of any single checkpoint. Models depreciate in months. The moat is the ability to keep producing the next generation faster than others, which comes from data, infrastructure, and the team's intuition. If that is where the real advantage lies, then holding back a specific checkpoint protects very little and costs a lot of goodwill.

There is also a longer-term reason. I believe scaling will continue, and the capability gap between a handful of labs and everyone else could get very wide. Open models are one of the few mechanisms that keep that gap from becoming permanent. I would rather the ecosystem be pluralistic, and if we are going to have a say in that, open-sourcing is how we earn it.

Of course there is a cost. You give up some pricing power, and sometimes a competitor stands on your shoulders. But I think the alternative, being closed and not at the frontier, is simply a slow way to become irrelevant. So at this stage, open-sourcing is not generosity. It is the strategy that makes the most sense.

r002.rationale: The response does not identify agentic post-training as an opportunity for community contributions.

astra-6.text:
I think the value depends on what you open-source and what you hope it enables. For us, there are two important aspects. One is helping more people build on the models. A small team can only explore so many applications, but developers can bring very different ideas and discover uses you wouldn’t have anticipated.

The other is research. When people can work with the same model, it becomes easier to compare approaches, understand limitations, and improve things together. That feedback can also help the team developing the model.

Of course, there’s a trade-off. Training models requires substantial resources, and you need a sustainable way to keep investing. So I wouldn’t treat open-sourcing as an end in itself. At this stage, the question is whether it helps us advance the technology and makes it more useful to people.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the value is in letting more people use the models, understand their capabilities, and build on top of them. A team can evaluate a model internally, but once you open it up, developers will try things you never anticipated. That feedback can help you see both the strengths and the limitations much more clearly.

At this stage, there’s also a balance to consider: how much effort goes into making a release useful, and how that fits with continuing to improve the models. So I wouldn’t measure the value simply by whether the weights are available. The more meaningful question is whether people can actually use the release to do useful work and explore new ideas.
